catalog_locator: Lindstrom 1995: sec. 2.1 'Word stress', p. 845 (Rosetta Project / archive.org excerpt of the CAD entry). Corroboration: Lindstrom 1986, p. vii (Orthography); Lynch 2001, sec. 1.5.2, p. 9, and sec. 4.4.3, p. 117.
catalog_quote: 2.1 Word stress. Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of words, except in a few exceptional circumstances. Where /h/ occurs between identical vowels, the first vowel is discounted in stress application. Syllables are stressed irregularly if they include underlying geminate vowel clusters. (These geminate clusters are not indicated here; see Lindstrom 1986 for relevant description.) (1) 'kətaha 'we (plural inclusive)' / -'uwehe 'come' / ni'amaha 'anger' / neni'mē- 'eye, face' / kʷani'hī- 'penis' [Lindstrom 1995: 845]. — Lindstrom 1986: vii: Stress generally occurs on the second last syllable of a word. This dictionary differs from Lynch (1977, 1982) in not representing the presence of geminate vowel clusters which, when in a final syllable, cause that syllable to be irregularly stressed. Instead, the symbol ' indicates stress falling irregularly and also marks cases where i and u are pronounced as [i] and [u] rather than the expected [y] and [w]. — Lynch 2001: 9 (Anejom and the Tanna languages, family-level): In Anejom and the Tanna languages, it is normally penultimate, but (a) final if the vowel of the final syllable is long, and (b) antepenultimate in certain very restricted contexts. Secondary stress normally occurs two syllables to the left of the primary-stressed syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the word. Two exceptions: (i) in a sequence V-h-V with identical vowels, the first vowel is skipped when counting syllables from the right (so ni'amaha, kʷani'hī-); (ii) words containing an underlying geminate (long) vowel cluster are stressed 'irregularly' — per Lindstrom 1986 p. vii, a final syllable with a geminate vowel takes the stress, and the dictionary marks such words lexically with an apostrophe instead of writing the long vowel. Lynch 2001 (p. 9) restates this for all Tanna languages as: penultimate, but final if the final-syllable vowel is long, antepenultimate in very restricted contexts. A weight-sensitive coding (long final vowel attracts stress) is a defensible alternative reading; Lindstrom's own framing treats the long-vowel cases as lexical irregularities against a penultimate default.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned by Lindstrom 1986/1995. Lynch 2001, p. 9 (family-level statement for Anejom and the Tanna languages): 'Secondary stress normally occurs two syllables to the left of the primary-stressed syllable.'
new_statements.exceptions: (a) /h/ between identical vowels: first vowel discounted; (b) syllables with underlying geminate vowel clusters stressed irregularly — in final position they attract stress (Lindstrom 1986 p. vii); (c) Lynch 2001 p. 9 adds 'antepenultimate in certain very restricted contexts' for Tanna languages generally, unspecified for Kwamera.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('words'); examples are citation forms including bound stems (neni'mē- 'eye, face', kʷani'hī- 'penis') and verb roots with hyphen (-'uwehe). Data from the Samaria village communalect (Lindstrom 1995 p. 844); no phrase-level statement.
new_statements.identity_note: Lindstrom's data are from the Samaria village communalect of Kwamera (south-east Tanna), which he says is representative; speakers call the language Nɨfe / Nɨnɨnɨfe. Same language as Glottolog kwam1252 (ISO tnk). Lynch 2001's stress statement is at the level of 'the Tanna languages' (Kwamera, Lenakel, SW Tanna, Whitesands, North Tanna), not Kwamera-specific.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the word; words ending in VhV(C) are stressed on the antepenult (i.e. the vowel after /h/ does not count), per the snippet. The snippet is cut off before anything on geminate vowels or secondary stress.

new_statements.identity_note: Lynch 1982 covers South-West Tanna (Nɨvhaal dialect primarily; Nelpwaai and Nɨvai noted), Lynch 1978 covers Lenakel; both are sister Tanna languages, not Kwamera. Lynch & Crowley 2001:129-130 note that Kwamera has several dialects and that the Port Resolution dialect is 'quite distinct'; the existing Lindstrom statements are based on fieldwork at Samaria village (per rosettaproject_tnk_detail-1). The Lindstrom & Lynch 1994 snippet does not say which dialect it describes.

sources.note: Sec. 1.5.2, p. 9 (family-level, covering the Tanna languages incl. Kwamera): 'In Anejom and the Tanna languages, it [primary stress] is normally penultimate, but (a) final if the vowel of the final syllable is long, and (b) antepenultimate in certain very restricted contexts. Secondary stress normally occurs two syllables to the left of the primary-stressed syllable.' Sec. 4.4.3, p. 117: all modern SV daughters 'have regular penultimate stress'; final long vowels attract stress. No Kwamera-specific stress paragraph.
